topic: CSR vs SSR vs SSG — When to Use Each

questions.question: What are the rendering strategies in Next.js — SSG, SSR, ISR, CSR — and when do you use each?
questions.title: Nextjs Rendering Strategies
questions.direct_answer: SSG (static generation): HTML at build time, served from CDN, fastest TTFB — for content that's same-for-everyone and doesn't need per-request freshness (marketing, blogs, docs). SSR: HTML per request with fresh data — personalized or always-current pages, at TTFB cost. ISR: SSG plus background revalidation (revalidate: 60) — static speed with periodic freshness. CSR: browser renders after JS loads — highly interactive authed apps. Next.js lets you choose per-route.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: SSG (static generation): HTML at build time, served from CDN, fastest TTFB — for content that's same-for-everyone and doesn't need per-request freshness (marketing, blogs, docs). SSR: HTML per request with fresh data — personalized or always-current pages, at TTFB cost. ISR: SSG plus background revalidation (revalidate: 60) — static speed with periodic freshness. CSR: browser renders after JS loads — highly interactive authed apps. Next.js lets you choose per-route.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The decision table (the interview core):

```
SSG (build-time HTML → CDN)         — same for all users, rarely changes
  use: marketing pages, blog posts, docs, changelogs
  the output is a FILE; serving costs nothing per request

SSR (per-request HTML)              — personalized or must-be-fresh
  use: logged-in dashboards, search results, stock prices
  cost: server work per request (TTFB includes data fetch)

ISR (SSG + revalidate window)       — static speed, controlled staleness
  use: e-commerce catalogs, news feeds, top-10 lists
  first request after expiry serves stale, regenerates in background

CSR (JS renders in browser)        — app-like interactivity, authed state
  use: admin panels, editors, maps — anything state-heavy after load
  cost: blank until JS loads (bad LCP if overused)
```

The App Router syntax (how you actually choose):
```jsx
// SSG — default for static routes; dynamic routes generate at build
// unless they opt out:
export default async function Page() { return <Docs />; }

// SSR — per-request (or the route needs request data like cookies):
export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic';

// ISR — revalidate per fetch or per route:
const res = await fetch(api, { next: { revalidate: 60 } });

// CSR — a 'use client' component with useState: renders on the client
```

The hybrid truth (what separates candidates): real apps mix strategies per route-segment — a blog is SSG with a client-side search widget; a product page is ISR for the catalog data and SSR for the personalized recommendation; the checkout is pure client. 'Which rendering strategy?' is a per-route question, not an app question.

SEO/perf tradeoffs (the follow-up): SSG/SSR/ISR all deliver HTML in the first payload (crawlable, good LCP); CSR delivers none until JS runs. That's why content pages default server-rendered and only interactive islands opt client.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q{who is it for + how fresh?}
    Q -->|same for all, static| SSG[SSG: build-time, CDN]
    Q -->|per-user / must-be-fresh| SSR[SSR: per-request]
    Q -->|static-ish, periodic updates| ISR[ISR: SSG + revalidate N]
    Q -->|interactivity after load| CSR[use client]
    SSG & ISR & SSR --> H[HTML in first payload: SEO + LCP]
    CSR --> J[JS renders — app-like, LCP cost]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why rendering strategy is really a CACHING question (the mental model): every strategy is a point on 'where and when does HTML get built': build-time (SSG — cached forever), request-time (SSR — never cached), or time-windowed (ISR — cached with TTL). Next.js 13+'s App Router unified them into one fetch-based cache: each fetch carries its own caching directive (default cached; revalidate: N for ISR semantics; no-store for SSR semantics; tags for on-demand invalidation) — the route's strategy is the composition of its fetches' policies, not a page-level switch. This is why 'SSG vs SSR' in modern Next.js is really 'which fetches are cached and how long.'

The streaming boundary (the modern depth): RSC output isn't one HTML blob — it streams. Server components resolve and flush progressively; Suspense boundaries (loading.tsx files) mark the seams. The practical consequence: a slow data dependency in one part of the page no longer blocks the rest — the shell renders immediately, the slow segment swaps in when ready. This is SSR's biggest TTFB weakness (the whole page waits on the slowest query) fixed structurally.

The invalidation controls (the production close): on-demand revalidation — revalidateTag/revalidatePath called from a webhook (CMS publish → exactly the affected pages regenerate) beats time-based revalidation for content whose changes are event-driven, and it's the answer to 'how fresh is ISR exactly?' — as fresh as your events, with stale-while-revalidate in between. The debugging frame: DevTools' network panel on the RSC payload, plus the x-nextjs-cache headers, tell you which layer served a request — the practical skill when 'why is my page stale?' comes up.
